title.en: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life

text.en: Grandmother picks tiny stones out of rice before cooking. This is separation. We separate mixtures every day: tea leaves from tea, cream from milk, salt from seawater.

A mixture has two or more substances that are not chemically joined and can be separated. We separate to remove harmful or unwanted parts, to get useful parts or to get pure substances.
Handpicking removes large unwanted pieces, such as stones from rice. Winnowing separates heavier grain from lighter husk using wind. Sieving separates smaller pieces from larger ones using holes of a suitable size, like flour from bran. Magnetic separation removes iron from a mixture using a magnet.
Sedimentation lets heavier particles settle at the bottom. Decantation pours off the clear liquid on top. Filtration passes the mixture through filter paper or a cloth. The solid stays and the liquid goes through. Evaporation of water from salt water leaves the salt behind. This is how salt is made from seawater.
Churning separates butter from curd by spinning. Dissolving and filtering can separate sand and salt: dissolve salt in water, filter out sand and evaporate the water. We often use more than one method together.

problem.en: How can you get salt from a mixture of salt and sand?

text.en: Add water to dissolve the salt.
Filter to remove sand, then evaporate the water to get salt.

prompt.en: Explain how a farmer separates wheat grains from husk.

requiredIdeas.en: Wind carries away the lighter husk.

commonMisconceptions.en: Forgetting that sand does not dissolve.

points.en: A mixture can be separated by physical methods.
Handpicking, winnowing, sieving and magnets work on solids.
Sedimentation, decantation and filtration work for solids in liquids.
